lede: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are each built from smaller units, and knowing those units tells you what the molecule is for: burning, storing or building. Burning a weighed food sample under a tube of water turns that idea into a number you can calculate.
can: Name the smaller units of carbohydrate, protein and fat.
Sort starch, glycogen, cellulose and protein into storage or structural.
Calculate the energy transferred and the energy per gram of food.

text: Biological molecules and the energy in food

md: Everything you eat is built from three kinds of molecule: carbohydrate, protein and fat, each a chain of smaller units. Some your body burns, some it stores, some it builds into cells. In the lab you burn a crisp and measure its energy.

alt: Three rows. Many glucose molecules joined in a chain give the complex carbohydrates starch, glycogen and cellulose. Many amino acids joined in a chain give protein. Three fatty acids attached to a glycerol backbone give a fat or lipid.

prompt: Fats and oils are made of glycerol and ______ ______ .
explain: Fatty acids. Three of them attached to one glycerol — the pair of words is worth a mark each in a two-mark part.

md:
**Carbohydrates.** The **simple** ones are sugars: **glucose** and **lactose**. They are an energy source and can be stored. The **complex** ones are long chains of sugar units: **starch** (storage in plants), **glycogen** (storage in animals) and **cellulose** (structural — it is what the plant cell wall is made of).
**Proteins** are chains of **amino acids** and are the **structural and functional** molecules of cells.
**Fats and lipids**, including oils, are **fatty acids and glycerol**, used as an energy source and for storage.

prompt: Which of these is a complex carbohydrate used for storage in animals?
explain: Glycogen. Cellulose is structural and in plants; lactose is a simple sugar.

title: Storage or structural?
md:
**Storage:** starch (plants), glycogen (animals), fats and oils.
**Structural:** cellulose (plant cell walls) and proteins (in cells).
March 2026's Higher paper asked for exactly this split and most candidates could not give it. Two words, six molecules — learn it as a sorting job, not a sentence.

text: Prescribed Practical B2: how much energy is in food?

alt: A boiling tube of water clamped to a stand, with a thermometer in the water and a food sample held on a mounted needle burning beneath it, and the two equations for energy transferred and energy per gram printed underneath.

caption: Burn a known mass of food under a known mass of water, and measure the rise.

md: **The method.** Measure 20 cm³ of water into a boiling tube — 20 cm³ of water has a mass of **20 g**. Take the starting temperature. Weigh the food sample, set it alight in a Bunsen flame and hold it under the tube until it stops burning. Stir, and take the highest temperature reached. The **rise** is what you use.

prompt: 20 cm³ of water has what mass, in g?
explain: 20 g. One cm³ of water has a mass of one gram.

title: The two lines of working
md:
**energy transferred (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C)**
**energy per gram (J/g) = energy transferred ÷ mass of food burned (g)**
The first mass is the **water**, never the food. The food's mass only appears in the second line. Papers print the 4.2 for you; they do not print which mass goes where.

prompt: 20 g of water rises by 19 °C. The energy transferred, in joules, is
explain: 20 × 4.2 × 19 = 1596 J. Do the multiplication in one line on the calculator rather than rounding halfway.

md: **Then divide by the mass of food.** If that 1596 J came from burning **0.40 g** of crisp, the energy content is 1596 ÷ 0.40 = **3990 J/g**. Dividing by a number below one makes the answer bigger, which is a useful check: a small crumb releasing 1596 J means a whole gram would release far more.

title: Why the mass in the first line is the water
md: The 4.2 is the energy needed to warm **one gram of water by one degree**, so the mass beside it can only be the mass of **water**. The food's mass belongs in the second line.

prompt: 1596 J came from burning 0.40 g of food. The energy content, in J/g, is
explain: 1596 ÷ 0.40 = 3990 J/g. If your answer came out smaller than 1596 you divided the wrong way round.

md: **Burn more, and the water gets hotter in proportion.** Repeat the burn with 0.2 g, 0.4 g, 0.6 g, 0.8 g and 1.0 g of the same cereal and the temperature rise climbs in step. Plotted, the points lie on a straight line **through the origin** — and that is the one shape that lets you write **directly proportional**. A straight line that misses the origin, or a curve, is 'related but not proportional'.

alt: A graph of the temperature rise of the water against the mass of food burned. Five plotted points lie close to a single straight line that starts at the origin and reaches about 46 degrees Celsius at one gram.

prompt: A straight line through the origin shows what?
explain: Straight and through the origin: directly proportional.

title: March 2026 B1 Foundation Q2, March 2026 B1 Higher Q4(c), Summer 2024 Booklet A Biology
md: In March 2026 the energy calculation itself was answered well — candidates used the formula they were given. What they could not do was the biology around it: another simple carbohydrate, what fat is broken down into, and whether each large molecule is structural or storage. In the practical units, the recurring arithmetic fault is typing an average as A + B ÷ 2 on the calculator, which does the division first. **Check that a mean sits between the two values.**

prompt: Two results are 4.0 and 6.0 kJ. Give the mean, in kJ.
explain: 5.0 kJ. A mean must sit between the two readings.

md: **Why the answer is always too low.** Most of the energy released never reaches the water: it heats the air, the tube and the clamp, and some of the food does not burn completely. So the measured value is **lower than the true value** — an accuracy problem, not a reliability one. Shielding the tube from draughts, holding the food closer and using a lid all raise the measured value towards the truth. Repeating the burn and taking a mean does something different: it improves **reliability**.

prompt: A student repeats the burn three times and takes a mean. What has she improved?
explain: Repeats and agreement are reliability. Accuracy would need less energy lost to the surroundings; validity would need only one variable changed.

md:
Name the smaller units of **carbohydrate**, **protein** and **fat**.
Sort six molecules into **storage** or **structural**.
Calculate **energy transferred** and **energy per gram**.

A short question of six to eight marks built round a food label or a burning experiment, and in Booklet B a table, a graph with a best-fit line and two marks on reliability. The 4.2 is given; the equation layout is not. Stuck: write the energy equation out with its numbers in it before working anything through.
